title: Widows, Elders, and the Family of God
summary: Paul tells Timothy to treat the church's members as family: older men as fathers, younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters. He gives detailed instructions for supporting widows who are truly alone, insisting that families care for their own relatives and that younger widows remarry. He then turns to elders, who deserve double honor and fair treatment when accused, and adds personal advice to Timothy about impartiality, caution in appointing leaders, and his health.
story: Having dealt with false teaching and with Timothy's own example (chapter 4), Paul now works through the different groups in the church and how Timothy should care for each. This section runs from 5:1 to 6:2 and covers age groups, widows, elders, and slaves. The organizing idea is the one Paul announced in 3:15: the church is God's household. Families care for their own, honor goes to those to whom it is due, and discipline is fair. Much of the chapter concerns money and support, and it shows a church already doing practical, organized charity. It also shows the influence of the false teachers, since Paul mentions younger widows who have already turned aside to follow Satan (verse 15).
historical:
Care for widows was a mark of Israel's faith. The law commanded that the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner be provided for (Deuteronomy 14:28-29; 24:19-21), and the prophets condemned those who exploited them (Isaiah 1:17). The first church in Jerusalem organized a daily distribution of food to widows (Acts 6:1-6). By the time of this letter the church in Ephesus appears to have kept a list of widows it supported, and some of them seem to have had recognized duties of prayer and service (verses 5 and 10). The qualifications for enrollment, including an age of at least sixty and a record of good works, suggest a formal group with standards, somewhat like the lists for overseers and deacons in chapter 3.

The instructions on elders reflect the same concern for order. Elders who lead well, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching, are to receive double honor (verse 17). Paul supports this with two quotations introduced as Scripture: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4, which Paul also applies to ministers in 1 Corinthians 9:9) and “The worker is worthy of his wages,” which matches the words of Jesus in Luke 10:7. That a saying of Jesus stands beside the law under the heading of Scripture is notable, and scholars discuss whether it shows a written Gospel already being treated as Scripture or simply the authority of Jesus' teaching.
cultural:
In the Greco-Roman world a widow's situation depended on her family. A woman's dowry was usually meant to support her if her husband died, and her children or her own birth family were expected to take her in. A widow without family or means could be left destitute. Paul's rule that children and grandchildren must care for their widowed relatives (verses 4, 8, and 16) matched what pagan society expected, which is why failure to do it made a believer “worse than an unbeliever” (verse 8). The church's resources were for those who had no one else.

Younger widows would ordinarily be expected to remarry, and Roman law under Augustus had encouraged widows of childbearing age to do so. Paul's concern is that younger widows who pledged themselves to the church's service, and then wished to marry, would break that commitment, and that without household responsibilities some had become idle and spread gossip, possibly including the false teaching. The instruction about wine (verse 23) reflects ancient medicine, which used wine for digestive and other ailments, and the fact that drinking water was often unsafe. Timothy may have been drinking only water as a form of self-denial; if so, Paul's advice fits his rejection of false asceticism in chapter 4.
literary: The chapter is built around groups within the church. Verses 1-2 set the family tone for everything that follows. Verses 3-16 form the longest section, on widows, and it is carefully organized: true widows are to be honored (3-8), the qualifications for enrollment (9-10), the reasons younger widows should not be enrolled (11-15), and a summary rule for believing families (16). Verses 17-25 turn to elders: their honor and pay (17-18), accusations and discipline (19-21), and caution in appointing them (22), with a personal aside on Timothy's health (23) and a closing reflection that both sins and good works eventually come to light (24-25). The word “honor” links the two main sections (verses 3 and 17).

outline.t: Honor true widows; families must care for their own
Elders who lead well are worthy of double honor
Accusations against elders and impartial discipline
Caution in appointing leaders, a word on health, and hidden things revealed

doctrines.note: The church is a family in which members owe one another honor, care, and purity (verses 1-2). It supports those truly in need but does not replace the obligations of natural families.
Caring for one's own household is part of faith: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith” (verse 8). Godliness begins at home (verse 4).
Accusations require two or three witnesses, discipline must be impartial, and nothing stays hidden forever (verses 19-25). God's final judgment stands behind the church's fairness now.

words.note: Chēra, widow. In Scripture the widow is a sign of vulnerability, one of those whom God himself defends (Psalm 68:5). Paul distinguishes widows who are “truly” widows, left alone with no support, from those who have family or means.

Timē, honor, and also price or payment. The double sense matters in verse 17, where “double honor” for elders seems to include both respect and financial support, as the quotations in verse 18 show. The related verb opens the section on widows (verse 3).

Presbuteros, elder. In verse 1 the same word means simply an older man; in verse 17 it names a leader of the church. The overlap reflects the word's origin: leadership was first entrusted to the mature and respected.

Prokrima, prejudgment or bias, found only here in the New Testament. Timothy is to act without prejudging a case (verse 21). The charge is made before God, Christ Jesus, and the elect angels, underlining how seriously fairness is taken.

christ: Paul's solemn charge is given “before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels” (verse 21), placing the church's everyday decisions in the presence of the Lord who will judge. The chapter's care for widows reflects the compassion Jesus showed, raising the only son of the widow of Nain (Luke 7:11-15) and praising the widow's small offering (Mark 12:41-44), and it echoes his rebuke of those who used religion to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:9-13). Placing Jesus' saying that the worker deserves his wages beside the law of Moses shows the authority his words already carried. The church that belongs to Christ is to treat its weakest members as he did.

hard.q: Why does Paul seem so hard on younger widows, and does verse 14 require every young widow to remarry?
hard.a:
Modern readers can find verses 11-15 harsh, as if Paul distrusted young women. The context softens this without removing the difficulty. The enrolled widows appear to have made a pledge of service to the church, and Paul's worry is that younger women, who would naturally and rightly want to marry again, would later break that pledge (verses 11-12). He also reports a real problem: some had become idle and were going from house to house saying things they should not, and some had already turned aside to follow Satan (verse 15), likely by following the false teachers. Marriage, which the false teachers forbade (4:3), is Paul's remedy, not a punishment. Elsewhere he says that a widow is free to remarry and happier, in his judgment, if she remains as she is (1 Corinthians 7:39-40), which shows that he did not think remarriage was required in every case.

Most interpreters therefore read verse 14 as practical counsel for a particular situation in Ephesus, not as a universal law. The underlying concerns (keeping commitments, guarding against idleness and gossip, and protecting the church's reputation) still apply, but the specific arrangement belongs to a world where a widow's options were few.

questions: Paul tells Timothy to treat church members as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters. Which of those relationships is hardest for you to practice in your church?
How should a church decide when to help someone directly and when to call on that person's family to help first?
Verses 24-25 say that both sins and good deeds eventually come to light. How does that encourage you, and how does it warn you?
